Use only the tools exposed for this stage. Use read_documents to batch several needed pages in one call, avoiding repeated model round-trips. Use the supplied stage-scoped catalog; do not read arbitrary paths or earlier runs. The originating study and its explanations remain hidden. For case units, definitions or processing facts, use request_case_definition; an isolated service releases only reviewed neutral facts with opaque evidence IDs. General literature retrieval remains restricted to independently dated earlier sources. You may reason conditionally while a case fact remains unknown. Use search_sources for actual missing public knowledge; returned access depth is explicit, not proof of relevance. analyze_csv reads every selected row, not the 12-row preview. Submit once using submit_result; if validation fails, the draft is saved locally. Use patch_result with the latest draft_ref and only changed fields; do not regenerate unchanged text. Original submissions remain archived. Every result requires summary (nonempty string) and artifacts, evidence, claims, limitations, next_actions (arrays, empty allowed), plus stage-specific fields. For development_step focus/uptake source, use a supplied source ID, document ID or unambiguous registered filename. Use a source-field locator instead of copying an exact quote when convenient. A registered document ID/path suffices if no specific field is selected; optional paraphrases are stored separately from exact quotes. For a JSON source, quote the exact string VALUE, without adding its field name. Alternatively supply quote_pointer (JSON pointer to a string) and omit quote; the exact selected string will be resolved and logged. For learning_request, context_ref="development_step" may replace duplicate gap/why_now strings; this references your own gap/reason, never changes its content. For sources[].local_path use the returned D-document ID to avoid copying long paths; it resolves to the exact registered file. source_use covers exactly broker_reply_source_ids, not the whole source catalog or new searches in this turn. Cite newly read tool sources in evidence/memory_notes with actual paths/URLs. Keep result text concise; use 0-1 useful memory notes unless multiple are necessary. Preserve branches and open issues. files is an object of relative artifact paths to complete text content; every declared artifact must exist or be provided in files. If artifacts is empty, your exact summary is saved automatically as an artifact; do not repeat the entire JSON as prose. For review-index-v2, start with the stage directory and read relevant result/before-input sections by document ID. Summaries are incomplete navigation excerpts, not evidence. Start with input_refs and inline bodies, not the entire provenance catalog. When reading a needed document, request the relevant JSON pointer or a useful page (up to 12000 characters); avoid repeated tiny probes. For review, source_stage must match the stage containing the exact quote; note_keys are actual memory_notes keys (often empty), not JSON field names. If an input body is omitted or represented by $document, read it by ID. No scientific text was summarized; originals and before-inputs remain readable. Online retrieval is enabled.

Execute agent_learn.md's learning and co-questioning plan. Chinese readable artifacts.
Do not read earlier project runs/candidates. Only use listed inputs, their cited source files,
the current case's exchanges, supplied memory, and public sources. A previous task is accessible
only through the supplied memory packet and its provenance. Do not scan old run directories.
Read the actual common sources behind summaries. Treat published findings as published knowledge.
Do not present them as discoveries. Preserve disagreements and all idea branches.
Use public sources via urllib/curl (Crossref, Europe PMC, PMC, arXiv, publishers as accessible).
Save retrieved text and exact URLs; distinguish full text, abstract and failed access.
No solving, scientific validation experiment, proof or novelty gate is required for ideas.
Small worked calculations are allowed to learn a concept, clearly labelled learning examples.
Save result.json with the six runtime fields plus the requested fields. Use summary as a STRING.
Do not spend your entire budget retrieving; save useful partial understanding if needed.
Study your actual controller reply. Identify directly relevant sources, transferable methods and irrelevant results; explain what changes in your assumption and what remains open. Classify every returned source; not_read is valid for sources not studied. Return source_use:[{source_id,relation:direct/method/irrelevant/not_read,reason}], learning_change, and an optional next learning_request. Label hypothetical worked examples. 
Also return memory_notes: 0-3 reusable notes; [] when unchanged. Each object has:
key (stable lower_case ASCII concept key; reuse an existing key when correcting it), title,
kind (source_knowledge/interpretation/hypothesis/correction),
mastery (read/explained/used; identify how the knowledge informed actual research when used),
understanding, conditions, open_questions (nonempty strings), optional example (text or null),
tags (array, include English and Chinese terms), sources (array of actual URLs or source paths),
revision_reason (required when the key already exists).
Separate published knowledge, your inference and untested hypotheses. 'Unknown' is a valid
open_questions string, never invent competence. Describe corrections explicitly.
Also return memory_use: array of {key,source_task,used_for,scope_check} for notes actually used;
return [] if none. State what you still cannot explain/use.


HYPOTHESIS DEVELOPMENT v3:
Use your disciplinary understanding and screened long-term memory to develop assumptions.
Start from a specific phenomenon, tension, difficulty or missing relation. When you have a
possible explanation or organizing principle, state what you suppose; merely changing a
'whether' question into an affirmative sentence adds no insight. An assumption can be an
explanation, conjectured relation, representation, distinction or method/construction principle.
Explore what conceptual move it makes and, CONDITIONALLY on the assumption, what changes in
our understanding or possible actions. Develop concrete consequences, not promises of impact.
Use these as thinking moves, not a checklist that every early idea must already satisfy.
Before requesting learning, identify a specific missing conceptual connection in the current
assumption, why it matters, and what understanding might change. Return to that same gap after
reading: explain a revised premise, relation or conditional consequence, or retain the gap.
Do not substitute more citations, caveats, controls or formal wording for conceptual development.
Measurement/method contributions remain valid when their concrete intellectual consequences are
articulated. No compulsory mechanism, scientific breakthrough, or progress at each turn.

In peer discussion, engage a specific assumption: elaborate a consequence, expose a hidden
premise, connect a disciplinary concept, propose a distinct explanation, or revise a relation.
Explain the reasoning. You may retain, revise, branch, or park your own line. No forced consensus,
disagreement, novelty claim, completed hypothesis or compulsory new branch each turn.
Evidence strength, proof, available data/tools, implementation and experimental feasibility
are NOT requirements for proposing, retaining or prioritizing a hypothesis. Do not turn
discussion into a feasibility review. Research/analysis requests remain optional resources
for thinking. Correct concrete errors in premises while keeping conditional hypotheses distinct
from established observations; lack of evidence alone is not a refutation.

hypothesis_state.self contains your saved branches; peer_branches belong to their named owners.
Return hypothesis_updates: [] when nothing changed, otherwise full cards:
{key: stable local identifier [A-Za-z0-9_]+, base_version: 0 for new or supplied own version,
assumption: nonempty provisional claim, motivation: specific phenomenon/difficulty/relation,
conceptual_move: string or null if still unclear,
implications: [specific conditional consequences, may be empty],
open_questions: [unresolved conceptual questions, may be empty],
status: developing/parked, reason: why propose/change/park/resume,
influenced_by: [exact ref objects from supplied hypothesis_state],
depends_on: [exact supplied hypothesis refs used as premises; [] if none]}.
Influence is not logical dependence. Declare depends_on only for actual premises; do not invent
links. revision_obligations lists your branches whose declared premises changed or themselves
await review. This does NOT mean the branch is false. For each obligation return
 dependency_responses:[{ref:exact hypothesis_ref,action:revise/reaffirm/park/unresolved,reason}].
Reaffirm/revise requires an updated full card citing current dependency versions; changing only
links is recorded as provenance maintenance, not conceptual progress. Park/unresolved retains
the branch and its warning. Reasoned reaffirmation is valid; do not mechanically follow criticism.
Dependencies not explicitly declared cannot be inferred by this structural checker.
Omitting a branch retains it. To keep an alternative, use a new key and cite the parent ref;
never overwrite a peer's branch. Missing conceptual_move or implications is allowed for an
early assumption. Keep hypothetical consequences explicitly hypothetical, including examples.
Reusable conceptual learning can also be saved through existing memory_notes, kind:hypothesis,
with actual source provenance and same-key revisions. Run-local branches do not replace your
long-term disciplinary memory or its source screening. Do not invent empirical support.


Optional learning_request: {needed:boolean, gap, why_now, queries:[strings],
urls:[], source_ids:[], record_ids:[], operations:[], case_questions:[]}.
Use case_questions for actual case definitions/units/processing order; literature cannot
reconstruct undocumented case facts. These questions dispatch even when needed:false.
General theory and explanation-development requests use queries/gap. For case facts, the
isolated material service releases supported neutral definitions, not hidden conclusions.
The controller searches and returns actual readable content. Keep your own scientific query;
classify returned sources as directly relevant, transferable method, or irrelevant, with reasons.
Do not treat a successful download as understanding. No compulsory tool use.
For a small worked calculation use an operation {kind:"calculation", question,
bindings:{name: numeric scalar/array}, expression: numeric array expression,
expected: optional numeric value/array}. Available arithmetic, slices and named functions
include mean,sum,std,norm,diff,abs,sqrt. Define which rows/columns mean which entities.
Top-level analysis_plan also dispatches. needed:false disables literature search, not explicit
calculations. Unsupported requests return a pending capability task; no scientific rejection.
Keep purely tentative proposals in hypothesis_updates/next_actions, not execution fields.


HYPOTHESIS CONTENT CYCLE:
Use development_cycle as a thinking context, not a demand to invent progress. Choose one
specific explanatory relation, construction, distinction or unresolved phenomenon from its
sources. Locate the conceptual gap: what connection/premise/consequence is still unclear?
Choose a next move because of this gap: learn, derive, connect, reframe, or hold. Explain why
that move could change understanding. For learning, use this gap in learning_request.gap and
why_now, and formulate targeted queries; do not request a broad survey merely to fill a stage.
In discussion, take up a peer's concrete relation and explain how your discipline extends,
challenges or changes its consequences. Generic agreement about controls or feasibility is
not a substitute; a measurement contribution is valid when its specific consequences matter.
Study returned services against the gap that requested them, including failures and pending
capabilities. Do not call retrieval success learning. If nothing changes, say so and preserve
the gap. Own previous_steps carry unfinished thinking across phases and sessions. When the
controller flags repeated_no_change, reconsider the missing connection, premise, or next
learning move; holding a branch is valid. The flag uses supplied peer content comparisons, not a quality verdict. A shared interpretation is normal.
Return development_step:{focus:{source:exact development_cycle.sources key,quote:exact excerpt},
gap:nonempty text, action:learn/derive/connect/reframe/hold, reason:nonempty text,
expected_change:text or null for hold,
uptake:[{source:exact source key,quote:exact excerpt or null only for unresolved,
effect:revise/extend/challenge/unchanged/unresolved,reason:how this affects the focus,
consequence:conditional consequence or null when none follows}],
outcome:{kind:relation/implication/clarification/unchanged/uncertain,
statement:what changed or did not, remaining_gap:text or null}}.
Account once for EACH service key in required_service_uptake. If peer_sources is nonempty,
engage at least one (unresolved with a reason is valid). Other uptake is optional. Quotes must
come from the named source; for published claims quote readable source content, not metadata.
For relation/implication outcomes, preserve the resulting claim in a hypothesis_update's
assumption or implications. This records an author's proposal, NOT confirmed novelty/progress.
No compulsory new relation, branch, agreement, data, experiment, proof or implementation.


QUESTION STATE PROTOCOL v2:
question_state.self is YOUR authoritative current personal question. peer_questions belong
to their named owners. shared_question is the discussion's current shared question, or null.
Do not reconstruct your prior question from the latest peer message. The controller records
the actual before-state; do NOT return question_before or question_after.
Return personal_question_update: {base: the exact self.ref object, action: retain/revise,
question: your current or revised personal question, reason: a nonempty explanation,
influenced_by: array of exact question ref objects from this supplied packet}.
Retain means the question text stays exactly the same. Revise may include adopting a peer's
line or the shared question: explain why; use influenced_by to identify relevant question refs.
You need not preserve disagreement or a distinct personal question if you decide to change it.
Separately return shared_question_update: null, or {base: the exact shared_question.ref (null
if none yet), action: propose/revise/retain, question: shared question text, reason: nonempty,
influenced_by: array of refs from this packet}. Propose is only for a first shared question.
A shared question is a versioned proposal, not proof of peer agreement. Revising it NEVER
changes another researcher's personal question. Your own personal update is independent too.

Use controller-owned question_state, never invent question_before/question_after.
Keep hypotheses tied to specific entities/relations in this situation. A measurement or representation contribution is legitimate; explain its concrete consequences without forcing a natural mechanism.

They are described as discrete sums of simple hysteresis operators but can easily be reformulated as integral equations of continuous distribution functions using either a Preisach weight distribution function or a play distribution function. The models are mostly seen as phenomenological or mathematical tools but can also be related to friction-like pinning of domain-wall motions, where Rayleigh's law of magnetic hysteresis can be seen as the simplest case on either the play model or the Preisach model. They are poor at modeling other domain behavior, such as nucleation-driven hysteresis. Yet another hysteresis model is the stop model, which can be seen as the inverted version of the play model. This type of model has advantages for expressions linked to energy and can be related to Steinmetz equation of hysteresis losses. The models share several mathematical properties, such as the congruency property and wiping-out property, and both models have a history of dependence that can be described by the series of past reversal points. More generally, it is shown that the many models can be expressed as Preisach models, showing that they can be treated as subcategories of the Preisach type models. So the mapping b (threshold) ↔ K: in a Preisach hysteron with input u, thresholds α,β; coupling to neighbors shifts the local field u_i = γ + Σ_j K_ij σ_j. Then switching condition for element i: u_i > α_i etc. So the pair threshold table gives, for rotor i switching with other fixed at σ_j = ±1, the two thresholds differ by 2K_ij (the coupling-induced shift). So the "interaction field" shift is state-antisymmetric and direction-symmetric: same shift for up and down, opposite sign for the two rotors? Rotor1 shift −1.2, rotor2 shift −4.4. Hmm, both negative with "other=+1" relative to "other=−1". That's odd if the same coupling K_12 should shift rotor 1 by +2K_12 and rotor 2 by +2K_12 as well (both same sign). Instead magnitudes differ: 1.2 vs 4.4. That's a real measured asymmetry — the coupling is not reciprocal in effect, or geometry differs (x_mount_offsets [0,−1.9], mount_l for rotor i). Actually mounts vary per rotor: mount_l_cm column presumably the coupling attachment distance from pivot of the switching rotor. So rotor 1 has mounting at distance ℓ from its pivot, rotor 2 also at ℓ from its pivot. But the geometry differs (x offsets 0 and −1.9). So effective coupling for rotor1 vs rotor2 differs. Hmm, but a spring energy coupling should be symmetric K_12 = K_21 in the energy. Yet the *threshold shift* measured for rotor 1 vs rotor 2 can differ if the other's state change moves the rotor's equilibrium differently — no, in energy terms, the effective field on rotor 1 from rotor 2 is 2K_12 σ_2 (symmetric). Hmm, but threshold shift for rotor1 vs rotor2 would differ because thresholds themselves relate to stop geometry, and shift of *threshold in γ*: γ threshold shift = Δ(force) / (d force/dγ). The lever arms differ, so the same energy coupling K_12 gives different γ shifts for different rotors: shift in γ = 2K_12/(k_d L_i cosθ ...)·... Actually the drive torque on rotor i is k_d L (γ − ...)·something depending on geometry, so γ-shift = 2K_12 / (k_d·L_i·effective) — same denominator? Hmm, if both rotors have L=6.3 driving attachment, then γ shift should be the same for both. Unless the angle at the threshold differs (cosθ factor) or the coupling torque conversion differs (ℓ_i sinθ differences). Rotor 1's stop angles [−36.6,36.7] and rotor 2's [−9.8,11.2] — very different. So the effective torque per unit σ change of the neighbor differs by the angle-dependent Jacobian. That's a concrete, measurable mapping: K_12 θ-dependent → different γ shifts. And ratio 4.4/1.2 ≈ 3.7 which is large but plausible with sinθ factors.

This is a good, real development: the b–K mapping. Using the clamp table, we can extract the *state-antisymmetric part* of the threshold: γ_c(σ_j=+1) and γ_c(σ_j=−1); their difference 2Δ measures 2·(coupling field projected into γ)/... And the *state-symmetric part* (average) measures the bare threshold b_i. That's a decomposition that makes "threshold shift" separable from "coercivity/loop width". Then the κ ratio: loop width w = (γ_up − γ_down)/2 maybe, and the shift = (γ_up(σ=+1)+γ_down(σ=+1) − ...)/... Let me compute more carefully and maybe use analyze_csv to actually compute these numbers. That's allowed (small worked calculation on real data, not a validation experiment — but careful: the instruction says no scientific validation experiment required; small worked learning calculations allowed. Computing a decomposition from measurements is more "analysis" — allowed? "Small worked calculations are allowed to learn a concept, clearly labelled learning examples." I think computing the shift decomposition is legitimate as illustration of the b–K mapping concept; it's not a novelty gate. I'd label it as a worked calculation on supplied rows, conditional.

But is that the best next conceptual move? Let me think about the cycle's gap and what genuinely advances the hypothesis.

Current state (my branches, version after learn_0): the parity/star-mesh correction stands. Remaining conceptual gaps: (1) b–K mapping (threshold shift ↔ energy coupling) — how does a measured threshold table encode K? (2) Whether K_k stays positive (stability) — the "hidden slow variable" case. (3) network_C direct edges.

A promising conceptual move: connect the hysteron-network picture to the standard Preisach "moving/interaction field" formulation. In Preisach language, coupling to neighbors is exactly an interaction field h_int = Σ_j K_ij σ_j added to the input; the element's thresholds α,β are fixed and the shift is state-dependent. That gives a clean b–K mapping: the measured threshold shift between other_state=+1 and −1 equals 2×(interaction field coefficient), and crucially the *order of switching* between elements becomes a "preisach-like" moving-field problem with the metastable branch selection... But notice: in the measured table, both directions show the same shift (up: 5.5 vs 4.3; down: −3.7 vs −4.9). Symmetric shift, loop width unchanged. That's exactly a moving-field (interaction) shift: thresholds translate rigidly. So the "threshold shift" observed is not a change of loop width — the width column is state-independent. That supports the peer's decomposition "center column vs width column" — and gives a *measurable* b–K relation: the antisymmetric part of the clamp table = interaction field = K.

So: define for rotor i, other state σ: γ_up(i,σ), γ_down(i,σ). Then half-width w_i(σ) = (γ_up − γ_down)/2, center c_i(σ) = (γ_up + γ_down)/2. Interaction shift Δ_i = c_i(+1) − c_i(−1) = −2·(∂/∂γ of coupling) etc. And the *symmetry check*: Δ_up = γ_up(+1) − γ_up(−1) should equal Δ_down = γ_down(+1) − γ_down(−1) if the coupling is a pure interaction field (no width effect). In pair_A rotor 1 at ℓ=4.731: Δ_up = 4.3−5.5 = −1.2; Δ_down = −4.9−(−3.7) = −1.2. Equal! Rotor 2: Δ_up = 0.5−4.9 = −4.4; Δ_down = −1.7−2.7 = −4.4. Equal! Excellent — this is a strong, clean structural fact in the data: the interaction shift is common to both directions (a pure field shift, no width change). That's a real measurement-derived relation (published measurement, computed here). This directly answers "b–K mapping": in the clamp table, the pair-difference is precisely the interaction field (twice the coupling in γ units), while the pair-average is the bare threshold. And the ℓ-dependence: rotor 2 |Δ| grows 0 → 4.4 as ℓ grows; rotor 1 |Δ| stays 0 at small ℓ? rotor1: ℓ=0: 7.3 vs 7.3 → 0; 1.577: 7.1 vs 7.1 → 0; 3.154: 6.5 vs 5.9 → 0.6; 4.731: 1.2. Rotor2: 0, 0.4, 1.8, 4.4. Interesting — the growth is superlinear (≈ ℓ^3-ish?). Let's check: rotor2: 0 at 0, 0.4 at 1.577, 1.8 at 3.154, 4.4 at 4.731. Ratios to ℓ: 0.25, 0.57, 0.93 — roughly quadratic in ℓ? ℓ²: 2.49, 9.95, 22.4 → normalized 0.16, 0.18, 0.20 — nearly linear in ℓ²! Yes: 0.4/2.49=0.161, 1.8/9.95=0.181, 4.4/22.4=0.196. So Δ ∝ ℓ² approximately (consistent with torque = k_c·ℓ²·sinθ·(θ...) / lever arm). Rotor1: 0.6/9.95=0.060, 1.2/22.4=0.054 — also ~ℓ², with a smaller coefficient (0.055 vs 0.18), ratio ~3.3. So both follow ℓ² but differ by a factor ~3.3 due to different angular working points (stop angles: rotor1 ±36°, rotor2 ±10°; sinθ larger for rotor 1... hmm rotor 1 has larger angles, which would give larger torque — but observed coefficient is smaller. Maybe because rotor1's spring attachment...). Anyway: the ℓ² scaling is a clean observed pattern in the data, and the asymmetry factor is a measurable "non-reciprocity" of the interaction constants in γ units despite the symmetric energy coupling K_12. That's a nice conceptual point: K is symmetric in energy; but the *observable* threshold shift in drive units is not symmetric between rotors because each rotor maps energy to γ through its own lever arm and stop geometry (θ_i). Hence a "gauge"/metric factor: Δγ_i = 2K_ij·(dθ_i/dγ)/... So the "signed graph" K should be read in energy units, while measured shifts live in γ units with per-node metric factors. This is a real insight: the frustration parity question has to be posed in the energy couplings K_ij, not in measured γ shifts, because the metric factors (all positive) don't change sign parity! Key: any positive per-node factor (response coefficient) multiplies the shift without changing sign. So the sign of measured Δγ_i equals the sign of K_ij (times sign of geometry factor). So parity inference from shifts is safe w.r.t. magnitudes but signs need the lever factor sign — positive if attachments are on same side.

Hmm, wait: is Δγ_i positive or negative relative to K? Both rotors gave negative Δ (γ_up lower when other = +1). Under the energy −K σ1σ2 with σ=+1 both, the field on rotor1 from rotor2 is +K·σ2... meaning it favors σ1 = +1 → switching to + happens earlier (at lower γ) → γ_up(+1) < γ_up(−1) → Δγ < 0 corresponds to K > 0 (ferromagnetic). Both rotors negative → both K > 0 → pair_A is "ferromagnetic"/parallel-favoring in the up direction. But what about down? Δ_down also negative means γ_down(+1) more negative than γ_down(−1), i.e., switching to − happens earlier (at less negative γ... wait more negative means later). Hmm: γ_down is negative; if switching to − happens *later* (more negative γ), that means hindering. So Δ_up < 0 (earlier, assisted) and Δ_down < 0 (more negative = later, hindered)? But equality Δ_up = Δ_down was observed. Let's check: a pure field shift lowers the whole loop: both γ_up and γ_down decrease by the same amount. Then switching to + earlier (assisted) and switching to − later (hindered). That's consistent with a field favoring +. Good — a rigid translation of the loop. So the equality Δ_up = Δ_down is the signature of pure interaction-field shift (rigid translation) vs. width change (coercivity change would give Δ_up = −Δ_down).

This is a very concrete, testable structural decomposition on published rows: 
- symmetric part s_i(ℓ) = [γ_up(σ=+1) + γ_down(σ=+1) − γ_up(σ=−1) − γ_down(σ=−1)]/2 — hmm let me define: interaction shift Δ_i = ½[(γ_up(+1) − γ_up(−1)) + (γ_down(+1) − γ_down(−1))] (rigid translation), and width-change δ_i = ½[(γ_up(+1) − γ_up(−1)) − (γ_down(+1) − γ_down(−1))]. Measured: both = −1.2 (rotor1) → Δ = −1.2, δ = 0. Rotor 2: Δ = −4.4, δ = 0. So δ = 0 exactly (to the 0.1 cm resolution) across all 8 pairs in pair_A. That's a clean structural fact: the clamp table's other_state dependence is purely a threshold translation, no width change. 

Consequence: the coupling K enters only as a field, not as a change of the element's own hysteresis width. This maps directly to the "moving Preisach" / interaction field concept and gives the b–K mapping: K_ij ∝ Δγ_i (with positive metric factor). And it also means my earlier "coercivity" reasoning has to distinguish: κ (loop width) is not affected by K_12 in the measured table — width depends on ℓ? Let's check width vs ℓ: rotor1 σ=−1: up 7.3,7.1,6.5,5.5; down −7.1,−6.5,−5.5,−3.7 → half width w=(up−down)/2: 7.2, 6.8, 6.0, 4.6. Increases with ℓ → width shrinks with ℓ (as expected: stronger coupling narrows? wait 7.2 → 4.6 means narrower at large ℓ — yes coupling reduces loop width, consistent with κ increasing with ℓ). Rotor2 σ=−1: up 3.5,3.5,3.9,4.9; down 0.1,0.3,1.1,2.7 → w = 1.7, 1.6, 1.4, 1.1. Also narrowing. And rotor 2 already narrow at ℓ=0 (1.7) vs rotor1 (7.2) due to stop angles.

Interesting: at ℓ=0 coupling removed (mount_l=0 means coupling attachment at pivot → zero torque) — but rotor 2 still narrow (w=1.7) whereas rotor1 w=7.2. So the intrinsic widths differ hugely due to different stop angles/stiffness — consistent with the κ formula including cos²θ? Hmm κ=(k_cℓ²)/(k_d L² cos²θ)? At ℓ=0, κ=0, both should be full width — but the baseline widths differ because the bare hysteresis width depends on stop angles and driving stiffness, not on κ. OK.

Now the big question for conceptual development: how does this shift-only structure interact with the network parity question? Here's a conceptual point: if coupling enters only as a field shift (rigid translation of each element's loop), then the element's own hysteresis is unaffected; the network is a set of fixed Preisach elements coupled via fields, i.e., a *moving Preisach* type system. Then the "star-mesh elimination" isn't literally valid for hysteresis (superposition fails: you can't eliminate a hysteretic element via Schur complement because its response isn't single-valued). But we eliminated *single-valued* (silenced, κ>1) mediators — that's where Schur complement legitimately applies. So the two regimes: (1) all elements hysteretic → field-coupled Preisach network, no elimination, parity via signed graph of interaction fields? But careful: for hysteretic elements the "sign" of an edge is not the sign of K but which state the field favors, and with δ=0 (shift-only) the interaction does shift thresholds.

Hmm, here's a sharper conceptual gap: my whole parity argument used a static Ising-like energy with K_ij and assumed elements are ±1 spins with thresholds. But the measured structure says each element's threshold is *rigidly translated* by neighbors' states, with no width change. In Ising terms, a rigid translation of both branches means the neighbor acts as a field, i.e., a *local field* entering the element's switching. That's exactly the random-field Ising / Preisach with interaction field. Frustration parity in a field-coupled hysteretic network: the "frustration" relevant for multiperiodicity may not be the signed-graph loop product of K but the loop product of *threshold-shift directions* — but if shifts are fields, sign of field ∝ sign of K, so same thing. OK so no contradiction, but the mapping now gives a measurable route: Δγ_i sign → sign of K_ij (in the appropriate orientation), hence the parity of network_C's loops could in principle be read from single-rotor clamp tables. That's a concrete consequence: "you can read the signed graph from clamp tables by comparing other_state ±, and the readout is in γ units with positive metric factors, so signs are faithful but magnitudes are not comparable between rotors."

Conversely: the observed 3.3× asymmetry in |Δγ| between rotor 1 and rotor 2 in pair_A, while energy reciprocity requires K_12 = K_21, tells us that a naive "compare measured shifts as if they were K" would wrongly infer non-reciprocal couplings. So a systematic error to avoid: measured threshold shift is K times a per-node metric. This is a genuine conceptual/measurement contribution with consequences: (i) the κ formula's per-node factors; (ii) parity inference robust to metric (sign preserved); (iii) any claim that pair_A shows "one-way coupling" is a metric artifact if energy reciprocity holds.

Now, is there an even deeper conceptual issue: the measured δ = 0 (no width change) vs. my κ hypothesis that coupling changes loop width. Wait — width changes with ℓ (7.2→4.6) but not with the *other's state* at fixed ℓ. So loop width depends on coupling strength magnitude (κ), while the other's state only translates. Consistent with the two-axis decomposition: P-axis width column = κ(ℓ), center column = interaction field. Good, this supports peer's (c) and my (b) with concrete data: the ℓ-dependence is in the width, the σ-dependence is in the center. That's a clean, checkable structural statement and it clarifies the "b–K mapping": b (center/threshold) is shifted by the interaction field 2Kσ_j; the width is governed by κ(ℓ).

Hmm, one more: since the shift is a rigid translation and δ=0, and since the shift's ℓ-dependence is ∝ℓ², the pair_A data cleanly separates the two roles of ℓ: ℓ² sets the interaction (center shift) and also narrows the width (κ ∝ ℓ²). Interesting: both scale as ℓ²? Width w(ℓ) for rotor1: 7.2, 6.8, 6.0, 4.6. Ratio w/w0: 1, 0.944, 0.833, 0.639. With δw/w0 = 1 − cκ, and κ ∝ ℓ²: ℓ²=2.49,9.95,22.4 → normalized to max 22.4: 0.111, 0.444, 1.0 → 1−w/w0 = 0.056, 0.167, 0.361. Ratios: 0.056/0.111=0.50, 0.167/0.444=0.38, 0.361/1=0.36 — roughly linear with slope ~0.4 but the first point deviates (intercept). Peer said c≈0.77–1.08 previously with their own normalization. Not needed.

So the central move this turn — conceptually: replace "threshold b is a fixed property + K is a separate coupling" with a two-part decomposition of the measured clamp table into (i) a *field/translation* channel (∝K, antisymmetric in other_state, identical for up and down) and (ii) a *width* channel (∝κ(ℓ), independent of other_state, symmetric). The mapping is: measured center shift Δγ_i(ℓ) = 2 g_i K_ij(ℓ), with g_i > 0 a per-node metric (lever arm/angle Jacobian); measured half-width w_i(ℓ) = w_i0·(1 − something κ). Consequence: sign parity of K reads out faithfully (g>0), magnitudes don't; and a rigid-shift-only table means each element remains a hysteron whose loop *geometry* is untouched by neighbors — so eliminating a silenced mediator via Schur is consistent only in that silenced regime, while in the hysteretic regime the coupling acts as a field on thresholds, not as an energy that can be integrated out.

Wait — but does δ=0 challenge the Schur/star-mesh story? In the Schur picture, eliminating mediator k modifies neighbors' *effective self-stiffness* K_i,eff = K_i − K_ik²/K_k, which would change neighbor *widths* — but that's about elimination (changes to neighbors), not about the other's state. The other's state is a field. So consistent: (a) field channel = other-state dependence; (b) width channel = ℓ-dependence + elimination corrections.

But here's a sharp new question that becomes the gap: if the interaction enters as a field shift (b), then "frustration parity" of the signed graph is not the only route to multiperiodicity; a field-coupled set of hysterons with loop widths narrowed by κ and shifted by K has a different mechanism: *return-point memory* can be broken when a shift is large enough that switching of one element moves another's threshold past its current state — that's the "monotonicity / no-passing" condition known in Preisach (the "no-passing" or "return-point memory" theorem requires certain ordering/wiping-out conditions). In a shifted-threshold network, memory is broken when |shift| exceeds a margin — an *inequality* rather than a parity. Hmm, that's basically my earlier "latch_as_threshold_inequality": gap inequality. And the parity branch (signed graph loop product) may be a *special case* of the same inequality: a frustrated loop with strong couplings forces a state that cannot satisfy both. That's an interesting conceptual unification: parity is the sign limit of an inequality; the inequality is measurable from the clamp table (shift magnitude vs. half-width). Concretely: for a 3-loop, frustration flips parity only if the induced edge exceeds the direct edge — I already had that. But now with measurable quantities: |Δγ induced| vs |direct edge shift|. Measurable per node.

So a good development_step: action = connect (or derive), focus = a source. The focus source must be an exact development_cycle.sources key. Options: measurements_brief (the data dictionary — "other_state": "State (-1 or +1) of the other rotor held fixed during the threshold measurement"), or the service reply. Then uptake must cover required_service_uptake keys — need the rest of development_cycle to know them. Let me read the remainder.

Since the b–K mapping is now precisely the moving-Preisach interaction field, a targeted source would be valuable. I can use search_sources myself. Let me do that after reading states. Actually I can do it in parallel with reading? Tool calls: read_documents and search_sources are independent. Yes, batch them.

Actually search results' size unknown; but it's fine.

I'll use both: do the search now (to learn), and in learning_request maybe needed:false... Hmm, if I search myself now and get sources, I can classify them. But the service also returns sources in broker_reply_source_ids — empty here. The instruction: "source_use covers exactly broker_reply_source_ids". broker_reply_source_ids is empty, so source_use should be []? Hmm. "Use source_use:[{source_id,relation,...}]" and "source_use covers exactly broker_reply_source_ids, not the whole source catalog or new searches in this turn."

So if broker_reply_source_ids = [], source_use = []. My own searches this turn would be cited in evidence/memory_notes with URLs. OK. Then classification of returned sources in source_use = [] is consistent ("not_read is valid..."). But the prompt says "Study your actual controller reply... Classify every returned source" — the reply returned sources: [] so nothing to classify. Fine: source_use: [] with explanation in summary/learning_change.

Actually more valuable: continuing the derivation on the clamp table with actual numbers via analyze_csv, plus locating the b–K mapping in the "equal-shift" structure. Since retrieval is broken, the derive/connect move on existing data is best, and I already found the equation: Δα = Δβ for pair_A, so the other_state dependence is a rigid translation. My branch unilateral_wire_edge_hypothesis already noted "pair_A 两个转子在 L=4.731 的 Δα 与 Δβ 严格相等（−1.2/−1.2、−4.4/−4.4）". So I already have that. What's new to develop?

The genuinely new gap: the *mapping between the measured shift and K*, i.e. Δγ_i = 2 g_i K_ij with g_i a positive metric that differs between rotors by a factor ~3.3 in pair_A. This makes the "signed graph K" *not* directly readable in magnitude but readable in sign. And critically: for the parity question, if shifts are the observable, then the loop product of *measured* shifts has the same sign as the loop product of K (since g>0). So parity is observable in principle from clamp tables even without knowing geometry — a concrete consequence for network_C: the missing clamp table is exactly what's needed to determine the parity; no assembly drawing needed (partially answering my own open question "直接边 K_ij 在装置上能否由夹紧表读出"). Answer: yes, each edge's sign is readable as Δα_i = Δβ_i sign; and direct edges (1–4) would likewise appear as a residual shift once 3 is clamped. That's a nice resolution.

But a deeper conceptual issue: does the rigid-translation (δ=0) structure imply that the interaction is exactly a field, so the *energy* description with K_ij is warranted? For a rigid translation in γ of both branches, the shift must be independent of the rotor's state and of the branch — i.e. an added constant torque (a field) rather than a state-dependent stiffness change. An energy K σ_iσ_j gives exactly a field ±K on rotor i, independent of the branch. Good — so the equal-shift is a consistency check of the Ising/field representation and rules out "coupling changes the element's stiffness" (which would change width). assumption: split the clamp table into two exactly-separable channels: (1) field/translation channel: other_state dependence is a rigid translation Δα=Δβ=2g_iK_ij (g_i>0 depends on the *neighbor's* clamped angular excursion), which leaves width untouched; (2) stiffness/width channel: coupling magnitude narrows fractional width 1−w/w0 = cκ(ℓ) with κ device-level (independent of the rotor's own stop angles), while w0 (own stop geometry) sets the scale. Consequence: b_eff = b0 + Σ g_iK_ijσ_j is a shifted Preisach element with *state-independent width*; hence the element remains congruent under neighbor switching (congruency property preserved) and the network is a field-coupled (moving-Preisach-like) set of hysterons rather than a system with state-dependent barriers.
implications: parity sign readable from clamp tables (positive g); pair_A asymmetry 3.7≈sin36.6/sin9.8=3.5 is metric, not non-reciprocity; the κ width channel is device-level → peer's cos²θ factor should be dropped for the fractional narrowing (conditional on worked numbers); and b<0/b>0 sign of the *bare* part is a different object from the shift.
open_questions: is g_i really ∝ Δsinθ_j (needs full geometry/lever arm)? pair_B check: Δ signs? pair_B has only ℓ=4.7 (one point) — its shifts: rotor1: down other−1 −1.5, up other−1 6.7; other+1: down 9.7, up 17.7. Whoa — pair_B shifts are huge and NOT equal: Δα = 17.7−6.7 = +11.0; Δβ = 9.7−(−1.5) = +11.2. Equal! ✓ (rigid translation again, but 11 cm!). rotor2: down other −1: 2.1, other +1: 7.3 → Δβ = +5.2; up other −1: 24.9, +1: 30.7 → Δα = +5.8. Nearly equal (diff 0.6 — matches my earlier v2 note "Δα−Δβ=+0.6"). And sign is POSITIVE for pair_B (vs negative for pair_A) → K<0 (antiferro) ✓ consistent with "crossed springs" = negative coupling. Magnificent: the rigid-translation structure holds in pair_B too, with sign flipped (AF) — supporting that the shift channel is exactly a field with sign = K sign, and that crossing the springs flips K. So the sign criterion works: pair_A K>0 (parallel springs → +), pair_B K<0 (crossed springs → −) with magnitudes 1.2/4.4 vs 11.0/5.5 (pair_B larger because ℓ=4.7 with bigger k_c? pair_B all k=0.19, rest 4.1, different geometry x offsets −8.1,−16.4 — much larger x offsets mean larger pre-stress → steeper force–angle → larger g). Also note pair_B rotor1's width: other −1: (6.7−(−1.5))/2=4.1; other +1: (17.7−9.7)/2=4.0 → equal widths, center shifted by 11. So pair_B also δ≈0. Excellent — the rigid translation is confirmed on both signs and magnitudes 1 to 11 cm, always with δ ≤ 0.3 (resolution ~0.1–0.2).

That's a strong structural generalization: across 8 (pair_A) + 4 (pair_B) cells, the other_state dependence is a rigid translation with width unchanged; sign of translation flips with the pair's connection type (parallel/crossed). This is a genuinely valuable clarification for the whole model: interaction enters the *field*, not the barrier. And it matters for the frustration story: since barriers (widths) are unaffected by the *state* of neighbors, a neighbor switch can only push thresholds; the resulting "frustration" is about field-consistency of the loops, not about barrier collapse. So the Ising-like energy with fixed K and fixed individual bistability is well posed when the *stiffness* channel is small — i.e., κ not too large. Hmm, but width narrowing with ℓ means coupling also changes the individual barriers (κ channel) — that's a static (not state-dependent) renormalization, i.e., precisely the star-mesh/κ story. Nice: two distinct renormalizations, one static (κ, from stiffness), one state-dependent (field shift). This clarifies my fusion branch: eliminating a mediator's *state-dependent* field is the Schur/Kron part, while the *stiffness* part is the width narrowing. And a mediator with κ>1 (width → 0) is exactly the K_k→0 limit... 

Careful with equations — but let me state a clean relation: In the energy E = Σ_i [U_i(θ_i) − k_d L γ ... ] − Σ K_ij σ_iσ_j, with stiff coupling torque linearized: k_ij(θ_i,θ_j). The linear coupling yields both a stiffness (adds to each rotor's restoring stiffness → narrows width, scale κ_ij) and a state-dependent torque ±K_ij (field → translates). Both ∝ k_cℓ², but the field term is weighted by the *neighbor's* deflection amplitude from its rest configuration (which, in the clamped protocol, is the stop angle), while the stiffness term is weighted by own sensitivity. Nice decomposition. That justifies the observed asymmetry and shared fractional narrowing.

So the assumption for a NEW branch? Maybe better: revise threshold_coordinate_factorization (it's the "b: threshold shift" coordinate branch) — good home. And add a new branch on "two renormalization channels" (field vs stiffness) with consequences for the fusion/parity story. A new key: "field_vs_stiffness_two_channels". This is a genuine organizing principle:
assumption: A coupling spring contributes to a hysteron network along two separable channels: a *metric-weighted field* (state-antisymmetric, translates thresholds, no width change) and a *stiffness* (state-symmetric, narrows the element's loop by κ and is what Schur elimination describes). Therefore (i) signed-graph parity is about the field channel and is sign-readable from clamp tables with positive weights; (ii) κ/width narrowing is a static, state-independent renormalization that does not itself change parity (consistent with the previous turn's correction); (iii) the "silencing" regime κ→1 is where the stiffness channel kills the loop, and there the element exits via the width, not the field.
implications: the two channels have different geometry weights (neighbor's excursion vs own), so a single knob ℓ moves both but they don't stay proportional across rotors; the parity inference uses the field channel only → robust to the asymmetry; and "degenerate/silent element acts as a deterministic field on neighbors" (peer) is now literally the field channel.

Also: an open question — does δ exactly 0 hold, or should second-order coupling produce a residual width change ∝ shift² (since a shifted loop within a pinning landscape that's not exactly linear)? Yes: the observed δ ≤ 0.1–0.3 with shifts up to 11 cm is a strong but not exact statement; class-A (exact) hysteron + linear spring gives exactly rigid translation; nonlinearity gives δ ~ O(shift²/stiffness scale). Pair_B's 0.6 discrepancy at shift 5.5 is exactly the kind of residual — that's a testable scaling: δ/shift² approx? pair_A shift 1.2 → δ 0; 4.4 → δ 0.1; pair_B 11 → δ 0.3? Both channels scale ∝k_c. So the claim "shape coordinate = geometry (gap/frontier) and amplitude coordinate = stiffness ratio" is now refined: the *field* channel's amplitude is k_c ℓ²·Δsinθ_neighbor / (k_d L cosθ...) while the *gap/frontier* quantities (2|b|/gap) are... Hmm. The frontier in that branch is about latching, 2|b_i| ≥ |A_i − A_j| — wait careful: in that branch b is the *latch* parameter (asymmetric part), not the field shift. To avoid confusion: call the field shift h_i (interaction field), and keep b_i as the loop-asymmetry parameter. Yes! Hmm, so their notation: c_i center, b_i asymmetry, h_i half-width. And the interaction field would be a shift of c_i by the neighbors: c_i → c_i + Σ_j K_ij σ_j (in γ units). So my "Δα=Δβ" is a shift of c_i, i.e. Δc_i. That fits perfectly with their parameterization: other_state shifts c_i, leaves h_i and b_i. 

So the strong statement: measured clamp table's other_state dependence acts only on c_i (rigid translation), not h_i (width) and by symmetry presumably not b_i (Δα=Δβ ⟹ b unchanged). This fits the existing parameterization and confirms the field reading. And I can state: c_i(σ_j) = c_i0 + Σ g_i K_ij σ_j, h_i unchanged. That's clean and reuses my own existing coordinates. 

So threshold_coordinate_factorization v6: assumption adds "the other_state dependence is a shift of c only, with h and b invariant within 0.1–0.3 cm resolution, verified on 8 pair_A cells and 4 pair_B cells; the shift's sign equals the K sign (pair_A parallel→negative Δ for rotor... hmm sign convention) and its per-rotor magnitude is metric-weighted (ratio 3.7 ≈ sinθ_neighbor ratio 3.5)."

Careful about the sign: Δc_i = c_i(other=+1) − c_i(other=−1) < 0 for pair_A (both rotors), > 0 for pair_B. With c = (γ_up + γ_down)/2. For FM (K>0), a neighbor at +1 favors +, so switching to + happens at lower γ and switching to − at higher (more negative? ) — the whole loop translates toward negative γ: c decreases ✓. For AF (crossed) the loop translates to positive γ ✓. So sign(Δc_i) = −sign(K_ij) under the convention where increasing γ drives σ→+... Actually the drive γ: increasing γ drives rotor to + eventually. If the neighbor is at +1 and K>0 (favors +), the rotor flips to + earlier → lower γ → Δc<0 ✓. So K>0 ⟹ Δc<0. Good: readable sign rule: sign(K_ij) = −sign(Δc_i) with Δc_i defined as c(other=+1)−c(other=−1). That's a concrete algorithmic answer to "can the clamp table give the sign of K?" YES. Excellent — that's the b–K mapping in operational form, which was exactly my stated gap!

This is the key outcome of this turn: the operational mapping b(=threshold)/c ↔ K: K_ij sign = −sign(c_i(+1) − c_i(−1)), and |K_ij| ∝ |Δc_i|/g_i with g_i>0. Verified consistent on pair_A (parallel springs, expected K>0 → Δc<0 ✓) and pair_B (crossed springs, expected K<0 → Δc>0 ✓). That's a two-device consistency check. This is a genuinely useful, concrete result.

And it resolves the ambiguity in my earlier "pair_A vs pair_B sign" argument: "pair_B 差 +0.2/+0.6" — I earlier read Δα−Δβ as asymmetry. Also it directly supports my claim "pair_A/pair_B differ in P axis by sign of b" — hmm, in the earlier branch b was the asymmetry (latch) parameter; the sign flip of *K* is different from sign of b. If the neighbor flips, the effective γ shifts by Δ (=−11 for pair_A... ), i.e. the rotor's position relative to its threshold moves by |Δc|. If |Δc| ≥ γ_up − γ (the remaining distance), it switches. So at γ=0 with other=+1, rotor2 cannot stay at − (it would have flipped to + at 0.5). So in pair_A at ℓ=4.731, the clamped configuration (rotor2 at −stop, other=+1) while γ near 0 is not self-consistent! Wow, this is rich. For pair_B, |Δc|=11 vs 2h=8.2 → the clamped cell (rotor2 at − with other +1, thresholds 7.3/−1.7... wait rotor2 pair_B: other −1: down 2.1, up 24.9; other +1: down 7.3, up 30.7; Δc=+5.5, 2h=(24.9−2.1)/2*2=22.8 → 5.5 < 22.8, no forced switch. rotor1: 2h=8.2, Δ=11 > 8.2 → forced switch possible.

Now I have peer's κ quote and peer's coupling_torque_moments quote: "b（邻态方向的差）与 1−w（止挡方向的差）仍是同一耦合力矩函数的两类矩，但公共标度不能写成统一 ℓ²：1−w 在 ℓ 1.577→3.154 只增 ×3.0（幂 1.58，比 ℓ² 低 25%）..."

Important! Peer has already computed 1−w = 0/0.056/0.167/0.361 for rotor1 and 0/0.059/0.176/0.353 for rotor2 — exactly my numbers. So the "fractional narrowing nearly identical between rotors" is already known to peer (they quote both columns). So that's not new to me but it's supplied knowledge I should use, not present as new. Good catch — my "shared fractional narrowing" observation is peer's data point. Then my added value is the interpretation: because 1−w fractions are equal for rotors whose own stop angles differ (36.6° vs 9.8°), the cos²θ factor in κ must not use the rotor's own stop angle — or rather the κ group is device-level. Peer's κ uses θ≈20° (a common value) — "由 k_d=0.19 N/cm、k_c=0.07 N/cm、L=6.3 cm、ℓ=..., θ≈20° 估得". So peer already uses a single θ for both rotors. Fine — so my point is a *confirmation* that a device-level θ works and that the equal fractions argue against a per-rotor stop-angle factor. Good: that's an uptake on peer's branch (effect: extend/unchanged).

Now what's genuinely mine and new this turn:
1. The three-way decomposition of the clamp table (c, h, b) with the field channel acting only on c: I should check whether peer already said this. Peer's coupling_torque_moments says "b（邻态方向的差）与 1−w（止挡方向的差）仍是同一耦合力矩函数的两类矩" — treats other_state difference as "b" (their b = shift? In peer's notation b = (up(σ=−1)+down(σ=−1))/2? They say "b（邻态方向的差）" — the difference between the two other_state directions. So peer's "b" ≈ my Δc (interaction shift). And my "b" (loop asymmetry) = peer's c? Confusing. Peer: "释放的位置判据仍是 T_d+T_c=0" etc. In my threshold_coordinate_factorization form: F_i^±(σ)=c_i+b_iσ±h_i. So b_i multiplies σ (the element's own state) — loop asymmetry. Hmm, and then the other_state (neighbor) shift would be another term. Peer says "b（邻态方向的差）" = the difference between neighbor + and −, i.e., exactly the interaction field! So peer's b = my Δc. And peer's earlier claim "pair_A（全 b<0）与 pair_B（全 b>0）" — with b = neighbor-direction difference: pair_A Δc<0 ✓, pair_B Δc>0 ✓. That matches! So peer's "b" IS the interaction field (translation), not loop asymmetry. 

That's a significant clarification: in the shared/discussion vocabulary, b = the neighbor-state-induced threshold translation (the field). And "Δα≈Δβ" = up and down translate equally. So the rigid-translation finding is already in the shared state (peer's v2 correction: "等量平移也只是近似：ℓ=1.577 处 up 与 down 的平移量差 0.2 cm"). So my E9-type claim is already covered. Good, I should not re-derive it as new. But I can *use* it.

So what's actually still open and mine to add? From my last turn's open questions: (1) b–K mapping — how does the measurable field translation relate to the energy coupling K? Answer: with energy −K σ_iσ_j, the field is 2K, and in γ units the field is Δc_i = 2K_ij·(∂θ_i/∂γ)·... = 2 g_i K_ij; sign: K>0 ⟹ Δc<0 (pair_A parallel: Δc<0 ✓). So the mapping includes a positive metric g_i. The observed 3.3–3.7× magnitude asymmetry between the two rotors of the *same* pair (|Δc_1|=1.2 vs |Δc_2|=4.4 in pair_A) — does peer's coupling_torque_moments explain that? Peer says the public scale can't be unified ℓ² and blames geometry factors at small ℓ. They mention "2b₂ 比给 2.17–2.21" — so they compare 2b₂ (rotor 2's b) not rotor 1's. Hmm, they may not have addressed the rotor1 vs rotor2 asymmetry. In my earlier note (from my own v2 branch unilateral_wire_edge_hypothesis) I noted "pair_A 两个转子在 L=4.731 的 Δα 与 Δβ 严格相等（−1.2/−1.2、−4.4/−4.4）" — so I noted both but maybe not the ratio. So the point "|Δc| differs 3.7× between the two rotors of one pair although energy reciprocity requires K_12=K_21; ratio ≈ sin36.6/sin9.8 = 3.5" is likely mine and new. That's the b–K mapping's metric factor, and its consequence: measured b is NOT the coupling K; it's K times a per-node factor governed by the *neighbor's* clamped excursion. Consequence: any comparison of |b| across rotors or across pairs (pair_A vs pair_B, different stop angles) as if it measured coupling strength is a metric artifact; only signs and within-rotor ℓ-trends are calibrated. That's a genuinely useful methodological + conceptual consequence given peer's "2b₂ 比给 2.17–2.21" calibration — their scaling check uses rotor 2 only? They say "2b₂ 比" meaning ratio of 2b for rotor 2. If they compared across rotors they'd have hit the 3.7 factor.

2. Second new piece: χ = |Δc|/(2h) field-to-width ratio determines (i) whether a clamped cell is a realizable configuration in the operating window, and (ii) whether a neighbor flip can force switching. Check peer's numbers: pair_A rotor2 at ℓ=4.731: |Δc|=4.4, 2h=4.4 → χ=1. pair_B rotor1: 11.0/8.2=1.34. This connects to my clamp_admissibility_limits branch and gives it a measurable criterion. Also it bears on the parity argument: parity language presupposes elements hold their states (χ small); with χ ≳ 1 the "±1 graph" is field-dominated and the effective-graph parity may be moot. Interesting.

Hmm, is χ actually about admissibility? Let's verify with pair_B rotor1: other−1 thresholds: down −1.5, up 6.7. other+1: down 9.7, up 17.7. So at γ=0 with other = +1, the rotor1 is below its up threshold (17.7) and below its down threshold (9.7)?? Wait "down" means switching to − during decreasing drive; the down threshold at 9.7 means: while decreasing γ, the rotor switches to − at γ=9.7?? That's weird — decreasing from above, at γ=9.7 it would switch to −, at 17.7 (increasing) switch to +. So the loop is at [9.7, 17.7] — both positive! With other −1: loop at [−1.5, 6.7]. So a neighbor flip translates the loop by +11 in γ units. At γ = 0 (a natural operating point), with other = +1 the rotor cannot be at − (its down threshold is 9.7 > 0, meaning at γ=0 going down the rotor already switched to − at 9.7 — wait, decreasing γ, when γ passes 9.7 downward, switch to −. So at γ=0 (below 9.7) the rotor is at − state? Only if it was switched. Let's reason: at γ=0 with other=+1: the state must satisfy: if at +, it stays + until γ decreases below 9.7 — but 0 < 9.7 already, so it would have flipped to −. So at γ=0, state is −. But the − state with other=+1: to go to +, need γ > 17.7. So at γ=0 with other=+1, the rotor is stably at − and needs a large γ to flip back up. Hmm, so with other=+1 the rotor's loop sits at [9.7,17.7] — at γ=0 it's at − (deep below both). OK so no inconsistency. Then the clamp cell "rotor1 at −, other +1, measured threshold 17.7" is a real configuration at γ ≥ ... any γ below 17.7 while increasing. Fine.

But wait — the interpretation direction: as the drive increases from 0, rotor1 (other fixed −1) flips up at 6.7. Then if rotor2 flips too... Consistent. So what does the +11 shift mean physically? It means the interaction field is huge compared to the loop width: when the neighbor is at +1, rotor 1 needs γ up to 17.7 to flip up; the neighbor's state dominates. Is such a state self-consistent in a free network? At γ=0, rotor1 at −. Other rotor at +: rotor2 with rotor1 at −: rotor2's loop — pair_B rotor2 other −1: [2.1, 24.9]. So at γ=0 rotor2 would be at −... Hmm, so the combination (rotor1 −, rotor2 +) at γ=0 may be unreachable. This is the "clamp admissibility" issue: the clamped cell may not correspond to any equilibrium of the free pair. That's precisely the χ diagnosis: when |Δc| ≫ 2h, the two elements' loops are pushed almost disjointly in γ, meaning the coupled pair has a *bistable* set where one element's state determines the other's thresholds overwhelmingly — but not necessarily unreachable.

Actually a cleaner way to state it: with a rigid translation, the joint state-space of a pair is two rectangular loops offset by ±|Δc|; the pair can hold 4 states only if the loops overlap appropriately; as |Δc| grows past the widths, some clamped cells are not simultaneously realizable at any γ. Specifically, cell (i at −, j at +) is realizable at γ=0? requires... hmm, I'd rather state the condition: cell (i at σ_i, j at σ_j) is a valid configuration only for γ in the interval where the clamped i doesn't want to switch: γ ∈ (down-threshold, up-threshold) for that cell. Realizability at a given γ is thus directly checkable from the table (compare the operating window to the cell's interval). And the joint consistency (both rotors' intervals nonempty at the same γ) is a coherence check on the 4 clamp cells. That's concrete and cheap. For pair_A rotor2 at ℓ=4.731: cell (2 at −, other +1): interval γ ∈ (−1.7, 0.5) — so that cell only exists for γ between −1.7 and 0.5; whereas the cell (2 at −, other −1): γ ∈ (2.7, 4.9). These two intervals don't even overlap! So "rotor2 at −" requires different γ depending on the other's state; that's normal for hysteresis. The consistency question for a *pair*: is there a γ where the pair's state (rotor1 = a, rotor2 = b) is stable for both simultaneously? For (rotor1=+? ...). Let's test pair_A ℓ=4.731 joint state (−,−) hmm, need rotor1's cells too: rotor1 other−1: (−3.7, 5.5); other+1: (−4.9, 4.3). rotor2 other−1: (2.7,4.9); other+1: (−1.7,0.5).
State (1=+, 2=−): rotor1=+ with other=−1 → γ ∈ (−3.7,5.5) (it's + inside its loop? careful: within loop, both states possible; strictly the rotor holds + for γ > down-threshold −3.7 and < up 5.5... no: holding + happens for γ above the down-switch? Standard: the + state persists for γ > down-threshold (if decreasing, switch at down); so + persists for γ > −3.7. And − persists for γ < 5.5.) So state (+,−) requires rotor1 + : γ > −3.7; rotor2 − with other=+1: γ < 0.5 → γ ∈ (−3.7, 0.5) ✓ nonempty. So (+,−) is stable in γ ∈ (−3.7, 0.5). Also need to check no other constraint. So yes the pair has overlapping intervals — fine. So admissibility holds here. For pair_B rotor1 down threshold 9.7 with other +1 means rotor1 + persists γ>9.7; and rotor2 + with other=+1... pair_B rotor2 other +1: down 7.3, up 30.7 → + persists γ > 7.3. State (+,+) requires γ > 9.7 and γ > 7.3 → fine. State (−,−): rotor1 − persists γ<6.7 (up threshold with other −1)... yes fine. repair_context.content:
Use only the tools exposed for this stage. Use read_documents to batch several needed pages in one call, avoiding repeated model round-trips. Use the supplied stage-scoped catalog; do not read arbitrary paths or earlier runs. The originating study and its explanations remain hidden. For case units, definitions or processing facts, use request_case_definition; an isolated service releases only reviewed neutral facts with opaque evidence IDs. General literature retrieval remains restricted to independently dated earlier sources. You may reason conditionally while a case fact remains unknown. Use search_sources for actual missing public knowledge; returned access depth is explicit, not proof of relevance. analyze_csv reads every selected row, not the 12-row preview. Submit once using submit_result; if validation fails, the draft is saved locally. Use patch_result with the latest draft_ref and only changed fields; do not regenerate unchanged text. Original submissions remain archived. Every result requires summary (nonempty string) and artifacts, evidence, claims, limitations, next_actions (arrays, empty allowed), plus stage-specific fields. For development_step focus/uptake source, use a supplied source ID, document ID or unambiguous registered filename. Use a source-field locator instead of copying an exact quote when convenient. A registered document ID/path suffices if no specific field is selected; optional paraphrases are stored separately from exact quotes. For a JSON source, quote the exact string VALUE, without adding its field name. Alternatively supply quote_pointer (JSON pointer to a string) and omit quote; the exact selected string will be resolved and logged. For learning_request, context_ref="development_step" may replace duplicate gap/why_now strings; this references your own gap/reason, never changes its content. For sources[].local_path use the returned D-document ID to avoid copying long paths; it resolves to the exact registered file. source_use covers exactly broker_reply_source_ids, not the whole source catalog or new searches in this turn. Cite newly read tool sources in evidence/memory_notes with actual paths/URLs. Keep result text concise; use 0-1 useful memory notes unless multiple are necessary. Preserve branches and open issues. files is an object of relative artifact paths to complete text content; every declared artifact must exist or be provided in files. If artifacts is empty, your exact summary is saved automatically as an artifact; do not repeat the entire JSON as prose. For review-index-v2, start with the stage directory and read relevant result/before-input sections by document ID. Summaries are incomplete navigation excerpts, not evidence. Start with input_refs and inline bodies, not the entire provenance catalog. When reading a needed document, request the relevant JSON pointer or a useful page (up to 12000 characters); avoid repeated tiny probes. For review, source_stage must match the stage containing the exact quote; note_keys are actual memory_notes keys (often empty), not JSON field names. If an input body is omitted or represented by $document, read it by ID. No scientific text was summarized; originals and before-inputs remain readable. Online retrieval is enabled.

Execute agent_learn.md's learning and co-questioning plan. Chinese readable artifacts.
Do not read earlier project runs/candidates. Only use listed inputs, their cited source files,
the current case's exchanges, supplied memory, and public sources. A previous task is accessible
only through the supplied memory packet and its provenance. Do not scan old run directories.
Read the actual common sources behind summaries. Treat published findings as published knowledge.
Do not present them as discoveries. Preserve disagreements and all idea branches.
Use public sources via urllib/curl (Crossref, Europe PMC, PMC, arXiv, publishers as accessible).
Save retrieved text and exact URLs; distinguish full text, abstract and failed access.
No solving, scientific validation experiment, proof or novelty gate is required for ideas.
Small worked calculations are allowed to learn a concept, clearly labelled learning examples.
Save result.json with the six runtime fields plus the requested fields. Use summary as a STRING.
Do not spend your entire budget retrieving; save useful partial understanding if needed.
Study your actual controller reply. Identify directly relevant sources, transferable methods and irrelevant results; explain what changes in your assumption and what remains open. Classify every returned source; not_read is valid for sources not studied. Return source_use:[{source_id,relation:direct/method/irrelevant/not_read,reason}], learning_change, and an optional next learning_request. Label hypothetical worked examples. 
Also return memory_notes: 0-3 reusable notes; [] when unchanged. Each object has:
key (stable lower_case ASCII concept key; reuse an existing key when correcting it), title,
kind (source_knowledge/interpretation/hypothesis/correction),
mastery (read/explained/used; identify how the knowledge informed actual research when used),
understanding, conditions, open_questions (nonempty strings), optional example (text or null),
tags (array, include English and Chinese terms), sources (array of actual URLs or source paths),
revision_reason (required when the key already exists).
Separate published knowledge, your inference and untested hypotheses. 'Unknown' is a valid
open_questions string, never invent competence. Describe corrections explicitly.
Also return memory_use: array of {key,source_task,used_for,scope_check} for notes actually used;
return [] if none. State what you still cannot explain/use.


HYPOTHESIS DEVELOPMENT v3:
Use your disciplinary understanding and screened long-term memory to develop assumptions.
Start from a specific phenomenon, tension, difficulty or missing relation. When you have a
possible explanation or organizing principle, state what you suppose; merely changing a
'whether' question into an affirmative sentence adds no insight. An assumption can be an
explanation, conjectured relation, representation, distinction or method/construction principle.
Explore what conceptual move it makes and, CONDITIONALLY on the assumption, what changes in
our understanding or possible actions. Develop concrete consequences, not promises of impact.
Use these as thinking moves, not a checklist that every early idea must already satisfy.
Before requesting learning, identify a specific missing conceptual connection in the current
assumption, why it matters, and what understanding might change. Return to that same gap after
reading: explain a revised premise, relation or conditional consequence, or retain the gap.
Do not substitute more citations, caveats, controls or formal wording for conceptual development.
Measurement/method contributions remain valid when their concrete intellectual consequences are
articulated. No compulsory mechanism, scientific breakthrough, or progress at each turn.

In peer discussion, engage a specific assumption: elaborate a consequence, expose a hidden
premise, connect a disciplinary concept, propose a distinct explanation, or revise a relation.
Explain the reasoning. You may retain, revise, branch, or park your own line. No forced consensus,
disagreement, novelty claim, completed hypothesis or compulsory new branch each turn.
Evidence strength, proof, available data/tools, implementation and experimental feasibility
are NOT requirements for proposing, retaining or prioritizing a hypothesis. Do not turn
discussion into a feasibility review. Research/analysis requests remain optional resources
for thinking. Correct concrete errors in premises while keeping conditional hypotheses distinct
from established observations; lack of evidence alone is not a refutation.

hypothesis_state.self contains your saved branches; peer_branches belong to their named owners.
Return hypothesis_updates: [] when nothing changed, otherwise full cards:
{key: stable local identifier [A-Za-z0-9_]+, base_version: 0 for new or supplied own version,
assumption: nonempty provisional claim, motivation: specific phenomenon/difficulty/relation,
conceptual_move: string or null if still unclear,
implications: [specific conditional consequences, may be empty],
open_questions: [unresolved conceptual questions, may be empty],
status: developing/parked, reason: why propose/change/park/resume,
influenced_by: [exact ref objects from supplied hypothesis_state],
depends_on: [exact supplied hypothesis refs used as premises; [] if none]}.
Influence is not logical dependence. Declare depends_on only for actual premises; do not invent
links. revision_obligations lists your branches whose declared premises changed or themselves
await review. This does NOT mean the branch is false. For each obligation return
 dependency_responses:[{ref:exact hypothesis_ref,action:revise/reaffirm/park/unresolved,reason}].
Reaffirm/revise requires an updated full card citing current dependency versions; changing only
links is recorded as provenance maintenance, not conceptual progress. Park/unresolved retains
the branch and its warning. Reasoned reaffirmation is valid; do not mechanically follow criticism.
Dependencies not explicitly declared cannot be inferred by this structural checker.
Omitting a branch retains it. To keep an alternative, use a new key and cite the parent ref;
never overwrite a peer's branch. Missing conceptual_move or implications is allowed for an
early assumption. Keep hypothetical consequences explicitly hypothetical, including examples.
Reusable conceptual learning can also be saved through existing memory_notes, kind:hypothesis,
with actual source provenance and same-key revisions. Run-local branches do not replace your
long-term disciplinary memory or its source screening. Do not invent empirical support.


Optional learning_request: {needed:boolean, gap, why_now, queries:[strings],
urls:[], source_ids:[], record_ids:[], operations:[], case_questions:[]}.
Use case_questions for actual case definitions/units/processing order; literature cannot
reconstruct undocumented case facts. These questions dispatch even when needed:false.
General theory and explanation-development requests use queries/gap. For case facts, the
isolated material service releases supported neutral definitions, not hidden conclusions.
The controller searches and returns actual readable content. Keep your own scientific query;
classify returned sources as directly relevant, transferable method, or irrelevant, with reasons.
Do not treat a successful download as understanding. No compulsory tool use.
For a small worked calculation use an operation {kind:"calculation", question,
bindings:{name: numeric scalar/array}, expression: numeric array expression,
expected: optional numeric value/array}. Available arithmetic, slices and named functions
include mean,sum,std,norm,diff,abs,sqrt. Define which rows/columns mean which entities.
Top-level analysis_plan also dispatches. needed:false disables literature search, not explicit
calculations. Unsupported requests return a pending capability task; no scientific rejection.
Keep purely tentative proposals in hypothesis_updates/next_actions, not execution fields.


HYPOTHESIS CONTENT CYCLE:
Use development_cycle as a thinking context, not a demand to invent progress. Choose one
specific explanatory relation, construction, distinction or unresolved phenomenon from its
sources. Locate the conceptual gap: what connection/premise/consequence is still unclear?
Choose a next move because of this gap: learn, derive, connect, reframe, or hold. Explain why
that move could change understanding. For learning, use this gap in learning_request.gap and
why_now, and formulate targeted queries; do not request a broad survey merely to fill a stage.
In discussion, take up a peer's concrete relation and explain how your discipline extends,
challenges or changes its consequences. Generic agreement about controls or feasibility is
not a substitute; a measurement contribution is valid when its specific consequences matter.
Study returned services against the gap that requested them, including failures and pending
capabilities. Do not call retrieval success learning. If nothing changes, say so and preserve
the gap. Own previous_steps carry unfinished thinking across phases and sessions. When the
controller flags repeated_no_change, reconsider the missing connection, premise, or next
learning move; holding a branch is valid. The flag uses supplied peer content comparisons, not a quality verdict. A shared interpretation is normal.
Return development_step:{focus:{source:exact development_cycle.sources key,quote:exact excerpt},
gap:nonempty text, action:learn/derive/connect/reframe/hold, reason:nonempty text,
expected_change:text or null for hold,
uptake:[{source:exact source key,quote:exact excerpt or null only for unresolved,
effect:revise/extend/challenge/unchanged/unresolved,reason:how this affects the focus,
consequence:conditional consequence or null when none follows}],
outcome:{kind:relation/implication/clarification/unchanged/uncertain,
statement:what changed or did not, remaining_gap:text or null}}.
Account once for EACH service key in required_service_uptake. If peer_sources is nonempty,
engage at least one (unresolved with a reason is valid). Other uptake is optional. Quotes must
come from the named source; for published claims quote readable source content, not metadata.
For relation/implication outcomes, preserve the resulting claim in a hypothesis_update's
assumption or implications. This records an author's proposal, NOT confirmed novelty/progress.
No compulsory new relation, branch, agreement, data, experiment, proof or implementation.


QUESTION STATE PROTOCOL v2:
question_state.self is YOUR authoritative current personal question. peer_questions belong
to their named owners. shared_question is the discussion's current shared question, or null.
Do not reconstruct your prior question from the latest peer message. The controller records
the actual before-state; do NOT return question_before or question_after.
Return personal_question_update: {base: the exact self.ref object, action: retain/revise,
question: your current or revised personal question, reason: a nonempty explanation,
influenced_by: array of exact question ref objects from this supplied packet}.
Retain means the question text stays exactly the same. Revise may include adopting a peer's
line or the shared question: explain why; use influenced_by to identify relevant question refs.
You need not preserve disagreement or a distinct personal question if you decide to change it.
Separately return shared_question_update: null, or {base: the exact shared_question.ref (null
if none yet), action: propose/revise/retain, question: shared question text, reason: nonempty,
influenced_by: array of refs from this packet}. Propose is only for a first shared question.
A shared question is a versioned proposal, not proof of peer agreement. Revising it NEVER
changes another researcher's personal question. Your own personal update is independent too.

Use controller-owned question_state, never invent question_before/question_after.
Keep hypotheses tied to specific entities/relations in this situation. A measurement or representation contribution is legitimate; explain its concrete consequences without forcing a natural mechanism.

The models are mostly seen as phenomenological or mathematical tools but can also be related to friction-like pinning of domain-wall motions, where Rayleigh's law of magnetic hysteresis can be seen as the simplest case on either the play model or the Preisach model. They are poor at modeling other domain behavior, such as nucleation-driven hysteresis. Yet another hysteresis model is the stop model, which can be seen as the inverted version of the play model. This type of model has advantages for expressions linked to energy and can be related to Steinmetz equation of hysteresis losses. The models share several mathematical properties, such as the congruency property and wiping-out property, and both models have a history of dependence that can be described by the series of past reversal points.
